title: Gen. Green Clay, the surveyor who built Clermont
summary: Green Clay came to Kentucky as a young surveyor, took his pay in land until he held more than 40,000 acres, built Clermont in Madison County, and held Fort Meigs in 1813.
bodyMarkdown:
Green Clay crossed the mountains carrying a surveyor’s compass and chain, and the chain made him rich. Born on August 14, 1757, in what became [Powhatan County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Green_Clay), Virginia, he apprenticed to a surveyor and was in Kentucky [by 1777](https://history.ky.gov/markers/county-named-1806-3). By 1781 he held an appointment as [deputy surveyor of Lincoln County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Green_Clay), Virginia. Kentucky titles were then a tangle of overlapping warrants and careless early surveys, and a man who could run the lines and file the claims could take his pay in land.

## Paid in land

Clay did. Through surveying and speculation his holdings passed [40,000 acres](https://filsonhistorical.org/archive/clay-green-1757-1828-papers-1780-1834/), much of it in Madison County, which Virginia formed out of Lincoln County in 1785 and [organized at Milford in 1786](https://history.ky.gov/markers/milford). He was a brother-in-law of [James Garrard](/people/#james-garrard), later governor.

Land led to business. By 1800 he owned [ferries, taverns, warehouses, mills and distilleries](https://grokipedia.com/page/Green_Clay). In 1798 he bought the Kentucky River crossing that Valentine Stone had opened in 1792, and it has carried the name [Clay’s Ferry](https://www.kyatlas.com/ky-clays-ferry.html) ever since.

Land also led to office. Madison County voters chose him for Virginia’s lower house and for the [Virginia ratifying convention of 1788](https://grokipedia.com/page/Green_Clay), where he voted for amendments and against ratifying the Constitution without them. Once Kentucky became a state he sat in both houses of its legislature, helped lead the 1799 constitutional convention, and became speaker of the Senate in 1808, the year he ran third for governor.

## Clermont

In 1795 Clay married Sally Lewis, and in [1799 he completed Clermont](https://history.ky.gov/markers/white-hall), a Georgian brick house on his Madison County land. Their sons included Brutus J. Clay and [Cassius Marcellus Clay](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cassius_Marcellus_Clay). The plantation depended on enslaved workers. Clay was [one of the largest slaveholders in Kentucky](https://grokipedia.com/page/Green_Clay), and he left no record of doubting the system his son Cassius would spend a lifetime attacking.

## Fort Meigs

In the War of 1812 Clay was commissioned a general of Kentucky militia. In the spring of 1813 he led a brigade north to relieve [William Henry Harrison](https://grokipedia.com/page/William_Henry_Harrison), besieged at [Fort Meigs](https://grokipedia.com/page/Siege_of_Fort_Meigs) on the Maumee River in Ohio. On May 5 a detachment under Col. William Dudley landed on the north bank, overran the British batteries and spiked their guns, then chased retreating warriors into the woods and was cut apart. Hundreds of Kentuckians were killed, wounded or captured in what became known as Dudley’s Defeat.

Clay’s own column fought its way into the fort, and when the siege lifted he was left in command.

The British and [Tecumseh](/people/#tecumseh) came back in July. Outside the walls they staged a mock battle meant to look like an attack on an American relief column. Clay [knew no reinforcements were coming](https://grokipedia.com/page/Green_Clay), kept his men behind the earthworks, and held the fort until the besiegers withdrew.

## Kentucky today

Clay died at his Madison County home on [October 31, 1828](https://grokipedia.com/page/Green_Clay), and [Clay County](https://history.ky.gov/markers/county-named-1806-3) carries his name. In the 1860s Cassius’s wife, Mary Jane Warfield Clay, oversaw the remodeling that turned Clermont into the Italianate house called White Hall, now a state historic site where [an early oil portrait of Green Clay](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:General_Green_Clay.jpg) hangs. The map pin marks the White Hall state marker.
